Sentence: And no doubt those things have exacerbated the decline in mental health.

Passage: Young people around the world are experiencing an unprecedented crisis of unhappiness and poor mental health. Many observers blame the expansion of social media that began in 2012-13, as well as the long-term negative effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on the social lives of the young. ___(1)___ . Placing it here creates a logical sequence: it first concedes the validity of these common blame factors before using the word "But" to pivot to the passage's main argument about deeper causes. This placement makes the transition smooth and effective.
The other blanks are incorrect. Blank (2) is illogical as it would insert the sentence after the pivotal "But," disrupting the contrast and backtracking to surface causes after the argument has already shifted. Blank (3) would incorrectly attribute "those things" to the list of deeper root causes, which are not merely exacerbating factors, and blank (4) is too far removed, making the reference to the initial factors vague and weakening the passage's conclusion about families.

Report 0 income.” Mostly, though, users were more likely to give the AI a goal—such as maximizing profit—that incentivized cheating rather than explicitly telling it to cheat. In a separate experiment, the team tested what kind of guardrails, if any, would rein in the AI’s propensity to comply with instructions to cheat ... The team asked OpenAI’s ChatGPT to generate prompts that could be used to encourage the LLMs to be honest, based on ethics statements released by the companies that created them ... [...] Past research has shown that people suffer a blow to their self-image when they lie. But the new study suggests that this cost might be reduced when “we do not explicitly ask someone to lie on our behalf but merely nudge them in that direction.” This may be especially true when that “someone” is a machine.

Because everyone then took artistic value to be a species of aesthetic value, artistic formalism could gain prominence only by dragging aesthetic formalism in its train. The explanation, arguably, has to do with the way aesthetic formalism honours the conceptual link between the aesthetic and the perceptual. Any adequate answer to the aesthetic question must meet what we may call the perceptual constraint, that is, it must plausibly articulate the sense in which aesthetic value is perceptual. It is not hard to see why Jamie Dimon owns a lot of shares in JPMorgan Chase. He is the bank’s boss and its shareholders want his interests to be aligned with theirs. Paying him mostly in stock, rather than cash, helps ensure that they are. An executive with a significant proportion of savings invested in their firm’s shares has tied their future to the company’s. It is rather more surprising that many mid-level bankers own a lot of their employers’ stock. Banks probably benefit from awarding them shares: as with bosses, aligning rank-and-filers’ interests with shareholders’ makes sense, especially when relatively junior employees can risk the firm’s funds and reputation. But the bankers themselves might well make their living from preaching the virtues of diversification to clients. This gospel says that tying your savings to your employer’s prospects is unwise, since you already depend on them for your salary.

At this point, your newspaper columnist [...] owns shares in his own publishing house. Worse, he did not even receive them as part of his pay, but actively decided to invest. Here, then, is why you should consider flouting the best financial advice around and buying shares in your employer. For a start, doing so might come with some psychological upside (provided you are not too troubled by taking unwarranted risks with your savings). Less is said about the quiet feeling that you are on the same side as your employer, rather than having been pitted against them. Worried that you are overworked for your salary, or that too little of your firm’s revenue flows into wages? Any gains are going to shareholders, so it helps to be one of them—even if you own too few shares to benefit much. The hedge might be more emotional than financial, but it is not nothing.

Then there are the more cold-eyed advantages. Suppose you work for a privately owned firm that is about to be taken over by a competitor. If you have spurned all offers to buy shares, the first you might hear of the takeover is when the rival company’s executives march into your office and start laying people off. If you are a shareholder, though, you might get some warning: no matter how small your holding, you will probably get a vote on the acquisition.

For some, investing in their employer might also be a rare opportunity to gain exposure to a kind of asset that they might otherwise have difficulty acquiring. Anyone can buy shares in JPMorgan, but buying private equity is more difficult for retail savers, even now that some barriers have begun to come down. Access to the high-risk, and potentially high-reward, leveraged buy-outs that powered the growth of private markets in the 2010s is still mostly limited to big, institutional investors. None of this means anyone should invest a big share of savings in their employer unless they are obliged to—especially if they work for a listed firm, with shares that confer fewer advantages. A small stake, though, might be worth defying financial advisers. And for your columnist’s sake, in more ways than one, please keep buying news from our publication.

options.label: A
options.option_text: A sculptor given fine marble but unable to carve it properly because they never learned the techniques of their craft.

options.option_text: A painter selecting striking colours but spreading them quickly without thinking about shape, proportion, or overall design.

options.label: D
